title: The Seven Guiding Principles

header.html: List the seven guiding principles; understand each principle and how it should be used; describe how the principles interact and work together
the official ITIL Foundation (Version 5) syllabus, version 5.0 (February 2026), category 4.2

html:
1What the principles are

Guiding principles are recommendations that guide an organization in all circumstances, whatever its goals, strategy, type of work or structure. They are universal and enduring. There are seven.

# Principle In one line
1 Focus on value Everything must link back to value for stakeholders
2 Start where you are Build on what exists; do not discard it without looking
3 Progress iteratively with feedback Small steps, with feedback after each
4 Collaborate and promote visibility Work together and make work visible
5 Think and work holistically Look at the whole system, not one piece
6 Keep it simple and practical Use the fewest steps needed for a useful result
7 Optimize and automate Improve first, then automate with technology
Exam tip

. Learn the seven names in this order. Questions give a scenario and ask which principle it shows.

2How to use each principle

Principle How it is used
Focus on value Know who the consumers are, what value means to them, and measure outcomes, not activity
Start where you are Observe the current state directly, reuse what works, and measure before changing
Progress iteratively with feedback Break work into pieces, improve in cycles, act on feedback, avoid a big-bang change
Collaborate and promote visibility Involve the right people, share information, cross silos, show progress
Think and work holistically Consider all four dimensions, the whole value chain and the wider context
Keep it simple and practical Remove steps that add no value, prefer the simplest solution that works
Optimize and automate Simplify and improve a process before automating it; use technology (including AI) where it helps people

3How the principles work together

The principles do not stand alone. They are interrelated and often used together: for example, start where you are and focus on value tell you what to keep; progress iteratively and collaborate tell you how to change it; keep it simple stops over-design; optimize and automate comes last. No principle is more important, and all may be relevant at once. [Verify live]

Typical trap: "automate everything first" breaks optimize and automate (improve first) and keep it simple.

Exam tip

. Scenario questions describe a mistake (big-bang change, hidden work, automating a bad process) and ask which principle was ignored. Name the opposite of the mistake.

Exam tip

. The principles are not ranked. Any option claiming one principle always comes first is wrong.

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1A team replaces its whole ticket tool at once, with no pilot and no feedback. Which principle did it ignore?

  • AFocus on value
  • BThink and work holistically
  • COptimize and automate
  • DProgress iteratively with feedback
Show the answer

Answer: D. Big-bang change ignores small steps and feedback.

S2Before building a new knowledge base, the team reviews what already exists and reuses the best parts. Which principle is this?

  • AKeep it simple and practical
  • BCollaborate and promote visibility
  • CFocus on value
  • DStart where you are
Show the answer

Answer: D. The team builds on what exists.

S3Which statement about the guiding principles is CORRECT? (1) There are seven guiding principles. (2) They are used together and interact. (3) Only one principle applies at a time. (4) They apply only to IT operations.

  • A3 and 4
  • B1 and 4
  • C1 and 2
  • D2 and 3
Show the answer

Answer: C. Seven principles, used together.

S4Identify the missing word(s). The principle "[ ? ]" says to improve a process before automating it.

  • AFocus on value
  • BThink and work holistically
  • CStart where you are
  • DOptimize and automate
Show the answer

Answer: D. Optimize first, then automate.

S5A department hides its work until it is finished and other teams cannot see progress. Which principle is it breaking?

  • ACollaborate and promote visibility
  • BStart where you are
  • CKeep it simple and practical
  • DOptimize and automate
Show the answer

Answer: A. Work should be shared and visible.

S6An approval process has six sign-offs, but two add no value. Which principle suggests removing them?

  • AFocus on value
  • BKeep it simple and practical
  • CStart where you are
  • DProgress iteratively with feedback
Show the answer

Answer: B. Remove steps that add no value and keep it simple.

S7A project looks only at technology and ignores people, suppliers and processes. Which principle is it breaking?

  • AStart where you are
  • BCollaborate and promote visibility
  • CThink and work holistically
  • DOptimize and automate
Show the answer

Answer: C. Holistic means considering all dimensions and the whole system.

4.2 Recall questions

R1How many guiding principles are there?

Show the answer

Seven.

R2Name them.

Show the answer

Focus on value; start where you are; progress iteratively with feedback; collaborate and promote visibility; think and work holistically; keep it simple and practical; optimize and automate.

R3Which principle says everything should link back to value?

Show the answer

Focus on value.

R4What should happen before automation?

Show the answer

Optimize the process.

R5Which principle warns against big-bang change?

Show the answer

Progress iteratively with feedback.

R6Is any principle more important than the others?

Show the answer

No; they interact and are used together.

5Quick Reference Card

Principle Cue
Focus on value link everything to stakeholder value
Start where you are observe and reuse
Progress iteratively with feedback small steps, feedback
Collaborate and promote visibility together and visible
Think and work holistically whole system, four dimensions
Keep it simple and practical remove what adds no value
Optimize and automate improve, then automate
